 Inspirational … Emma Fogarty and Colin Farrell in The Slightest Touch. Photograph: PR View image in fullscreen Inspirational … Emma Fogarty and Colin Farrell in The Slightest Touch. Photograph: PR The seven best films to watch on TV this week Television & radio The Slightest Touch to California Schemin’: the seven best films to watch on TV this week
 A heart-shredding documentary about the beautiful friendship between Emma Fogarty and Colin Farrell, and James McAvoy tells the cracking true story of two Scottish rappers pretending to be American
 Simon Wardell Fri 20 Nov 2026 04.00 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Pick of the week
 The Slightest Touch
 Emma Fogarty is 40 and lives with epidermolysis bullosa, a rare inherited disorder that makes her skin incredibly fragile, prone to tears and blisters. She’s also good mates with film star Colin Farrell. Rachel Fleit’s heart-shredding documentary follows their preparations for the 2024 Dublin marathon, which he plans to run before pushing her in a wheelchair for the final 4k. Fogarty’s resilience in the face of near-constant pain is inspirational but hard to watch, while Farrell reluctantly allows cameras into his private life, physically squirming at times as he opens up about his addictions, sons – one of whom also has a genetic condition – and his beautiful friendship with Fogarty. 
Thursday, HBO Max 
 Belle De Jour
 View image in fullscreen Porcelain poise … Catherine Deneuve in Belle De Jour. Photograph: Rex The centrepiece of an evening celebrating French national treasure Catherine Deneuve, Luis Buñuel’s 1967 psychological drama does its best to ruffle her porcelain poise. She plays young housewife Séverine, who is unable to have sex with her husband of one year, Pierre (Jean Sorel), retreating into bizarre S&M dreams. Then, she discovers that working at a Paris brothel may be a way of solving her intimacy issues. Throughout, arch provocateur Buñuel teases her – and us – with the idea that female freedom can come via being paid to fulfil male fantasies.
 Saturday, 9.40pm, BBC Four 
 Downhill Racer
 View image in fullscreen Heading for a showdown … Gene Hackman and Robert Redford in Downhill Racer. Photograph: Allstar Picture Library/Alamy Despite his pin-up image, Robert Redford was always interested in playing against that type. In Michael Ritchie’s crisp 1969 sports film, his American skier David Chappellet has the arrogance and selfishness of the good-looking and talented. But as the US team, led by Gene Hackman’s head coach Eugene Claire, race their way through the European season towards a showdown at the Winter Olympics, is that just the necessary champion’s mentality? Shot with a fly-on-the-glacier-wall feel, it’s a cool appraisal of the hidden side of athletic success.
 Sunday, 8pm, Sky Arts
 Give Me the Ball!
 View image in fullscreen Trailblazer … Billie Jean King in Give Me the Ball! Unarguably the most important female tennis player in history, Billie Jean King gets a profile that does full justice to her range of achievements. A multiple grand slam champion with a phenomenal can-do attitude, she led the fight for equal prize money with the men and basically birthed the entire women’s professional game. King is also a wonderfully eloquent and candid interviewee, so directors Liz Garbus and Elizabeth Wolff just set the camera down and let her tell all. Binge eating, sexuality, Elton John – just a few of the topics touched on in a remarkable life story.
 Monday, Disney+

 Way of the Warrior Kid
 View image in fullscreen Feel-good … Chris Pratt as Jake and Jude Hill as Marc in Way of the Warrior Kid. Photograph: Brian Douglas/Apple TV/PA There are distinct echoes of The Karate Kid in McG’s light moral drama, based on a children’s book by a former Navy Seal. Marc (Jude Hill) is being bullied at school in San Diego and has zero confidence, despite the best efforts of widowed mom Sarah (Linda Cardellini). Luckily, his uncle Jake (Chris Pratt) is coming to stay … and he’s in the special forces. Jake sets up a training programme for his nephew to boost his self-worth – and teach him a few moves – but the officer has his own demons to face.
 Wednesday, Apple TV 
 Cabaret
 View image in fullscreen The greatest of all movie musicals! … Liza Minnelli in Cabaret. Photograph: ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content/Getty Images Willkommen, bienvenue, welcome to possibly the greatest of all movie musicals. Bob Fosse’s adaptation of the Kander and Ebb stage hit adds now-classic songs (Maybe This Time, Money Money) alongside his distinctively slinky choreography, while Liza Minnelli’s Sally Bowles, the headline singer at a club in 1931 Berlin, is an American (not British) force of nature. Michael York co-stars as her love interest, English writer Brian, but he plays second fiddle to the Oscar-winning Minnelli, who owns every song and brings pathos to her tragic character – a creative soul about to be crushed by fascism.
 Thursday, 11pm, BBC Two 
 California Schemin’
 View image in fullscreen Cracking … Seamus McLean Ross and Samuel Bottomley in California Schemin’. For his directorial debut , James McAvoy has picked a cracking true story. Two aspiring rappers in 2003 Dundee – Gavin (Séamus McLean Ross) and Billy (Samuel Bottomley) AKA Silibil n’ Brains – get knocked back in a label casting call (“It’s the rapping Proclaimers!”), so decide to pose as American dudes to show up the biases of the music industry. They are an instant success – but how far can, and should, they take the joke? It’s a propulsive, music-stuffed caper that never loses sight of the emotional toll the scam takes on the two friends.
 Friday , 10.25am, 7.05pm, Sky Cinema Premiere
